blocks.text: 1. Query Transformation

blocks.alt: An original query goes through transformation to become a better-suited query

blocks.text: Query Rewriting covered replacing a query outright. Query Transformation names the broader umbrella category that both query expansion and query rewriting fall under.
It covers any technique that modifies a query before it ever reaches retrieval.
2. Naming The Umbrella
Query expansion and query rewriting are both specific instances of a broader category.
Query transformation names that broader category directly.

blocks.content: {"headers": ["Technique", "Relationship to query transformation"], "rows": [["Query expansion", "One specific transformation technique"], ["Query rewriting", "Another specific transformation technique"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Where Transformation Happens In The Pipeline

blocks.alt: A user query goes through a transformation step before retrieval

blocks.text: As with the end to end semantic search pipeline in Semantic Search, transformation happens after the user submits a query, but before embedding or search runs.
It's a single, well defined stage that any transformation technique plugs into.
4. Decomposition Into Subqueries

blocks.alt: A complex query breaks into subquery 1 and subquery 2

blocks.text: A complex question can be broken into several smaller, simpler sub questions.
Each sub question gets retrieved separately, then combined afterward.
5. Hypothetical Document Generation

blocks.alt: A query goes through an LLM generating a hypothetical answer document

blocks.text: Instead of embedding the question itself, a language model first writes a hypothetical answer.
That hypothetical answer gets embedded and searched with instead of the raw question.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: This technique works because a hypothetical answer often resembles the actual relevant chunk more closely in embedding space than the original question ever would, since both are written in a similar answer style.

blocks.text: 6. Step Back Prompting

blocks.alt: A specific question steps back into a general question

blocks.text: A narrow, specific question sometimes benefits from first asking a broader, more general version.
This retrieves background context before narrowing back down to the specific answer.
7. Choosing A Transformation Strategy

blocks.alt: Decomposition, HyDE, and step-back are transformation strategy options

blocks.text: As with the latency cost of expansion in Query Expansion, every transformation technique adds some processing time before retrieval.
Choosing the right technique depends on the specific weakness a given query actually has.

blocks.text: 8. Transformation As A Preprocessing Layer
Every retrieval technique covered later in this module can sit downstream of a query transformation step.
Transformation improves the input; retrieval and re-ranking, covered as the next module, improve the output.
9. Recognizing Which Query Transformation Fits A Given Problem

blocks.alt: A query not matching documents well points toward applying query transformation

blocks.text: Complex, multi part questions benefit from decomposition.
Short, vague, or ambiguous questions benefit more from rewriting or hypothetical document generation.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates decomposing a complex question into simpler subqueries.

code.content:
def decompose_query(query):
    # decomposition into subqueries
    if " and " in query.lower():
        parts = query.split(" and ")
        return [p.strip() + "?" if not p.strip().endswith("?") else p.strip() for p in parts]
    return [query]

complex_query = "What is the refund policy and how long does shipping take"
subqueries = decompose_query(complex_query)

print(f"Complex query: {complex_query!r}\n")
print("Decomposed subqueries (decomposition into subqueries):")
for sq in subqueries:
    print(f" {sq!r}")

print("\nEach subquery gets retrieved separately, then combined,")
print("decomposition into subqueries.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows a single complex question splitting into two independently retrievable subquestions.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Treating query expansion, rewriting, and transformation as three unrelated techniques.
Applying decomposition to a simple, single part question that never needed splitting.
Using hypothetical document generation without considering its added latency and cost.
Choosing a transformation technique that does not match the query's actual underlying problem.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Query transformation is the broader category covering any technique that modifies a query before retrieval.
Query expansion and query rewriting are both specific instances of this broader category.
Transformation happens after a query is submitted but before embedding or search runs.
Decomposition breaks a complex question into simpler subqueries retrieved separately.
Hypothetical document generation searches with a generated hypothetical answer instead of the raw question.
Step back prompting retrieves broader background context before narrowing to a specific answer.
Choosing the right transformation technique depends on the specific weakness a query has.
Transformation acts as a preprocessing layer that improves the input to everything downstream.
